# 深度研究报告：如何增强自闭症学生课堂参与度——有效策略与实践指南

## 1. 引言

自闭症谱系障碍（Autism Spectrum Disorder, ASD）学生在课堂上面临独特的挑战，包括感官超负荷、社交沟通困难、对变化的抗拒以及执行功能方面的障碍。这些挑战可能导致他们在课堂上出现退缩、焦虑、逃避行为或注意力不集中，从而显著影响其学习参与度。增强自闭症学生的课堂参与不仅是教育公平的体现，更是提升其学业成就和社交情感发展的关键。本报告旨在系统梳理经过实证验证的有效策略，为教育工作者、家长和学校管理者提供一份可操作的深度指南。

## 2. 核心策略：构建支持性环境

### 2.1 物理环境调整与感官支持

自闭症学生常对感官刺激（如噪音、光线、触觉）过度敏感或反应不足。一个“感官友好型”的教室是提高参与度的基石。

- **降低感官负荷**：使用柔和的照明（如用自然光、调暗灯光或用台灯代替顶灯），减少教室内的视觉杂乱（如遮盖不必要的海报、储物柜），并控制噪音（如允许学生佩戴降噪耳机、使用地毯或软垫减少摩擦声）。
- **设立“感官休息区”**：在教室角落设置一个安静、可遮挡视线的空间，配备重力毯、按摩球、耳机、沙漏等物品。学生在感到焦虑或过度刺激时，可以自主前往该区域进行自我调节，之后再返回课堂活动。这并非惩罚，而是赋能。
- **灵活的座位安排**：允许学生选择能减少干扰的座位（如靠近老师、背对窗户、教室边缘）。

> **关键事实来源**：美国疾病控制与预防中心（CDC）指出，为自闭症学生提供感官友好环境是有效教育策略的核心组成部分 [1]。

### 2.2 可预测的结构化日程

自闭症学生依赖可预测性来获得安全感。高度的不确定性会引发焦虑，导致参与度下降。

- **视觉时间表**：使用图片、图标或文字制作每日或每节课的流程表，清晰展示“现在做什么”和“接下来做什么”。流程表应放置在学生视线可及处，并在每项活动结束后手动更新。
- **提前预告**：在活动转换前5-10分钟，用视觉或口头方式提醒学生。例如：“还有5分钟，我们就要结束阅读，开始小组讨论了。”
- **建立常规仪式**：每天以相同的方式开始和结束课程（如早上的问候歌、下课前的总结清单），帮助学生平稳过渡。

> **关键事实来源**：美国国家自闭症中心（National Autism Center）的《国家标准项目》（National Standards Project）强烈推荐将“视觉支持”和“结构化教学”作为循证实践 [2]。

## 3. 核心策略：教学与沟通方法

### 3.1 视觉支持策略

许多自闭症学生是视觉学习者。视觉支持能将抽象概念具体化，弥补听觉处理能力的不足。

- **视觉指令与任务板**：将复杂的任务分解成几个步骤，并用图片或文字列出。学生完成一项后打勾或移走卡片。
- **社交故事与脚本**：使用简短的文字和图片描述特定的社交情境，帮助学生理解场景、预期行为和可能的反应。例如，针对“如何请求帮助”或“如何加入小组游戏”的社交故事。
- **行为契约**：与学生一起制定一个简单的视觉化协议，明确“如果我可以（完成X任务），那么我就可以（获得Y奖励）”。这利用了学生的规则性思维。

> **关键事实来源**：印第安纳大学资源中心指出，社交故事是一种有效的实践，可以教导自闭症学生在社交情境中适当的行为 [3]。

### 3.2 明确且直接的沟通

避免使用模糊的、带有讽刺意味或双重含义的语言。

- **使用直接、具体的语言**：不要问“你准备好了吗？”，而是说“请拿出你的数学书，翻到第20页。”不要“坐下”，而是“请坐到你的椅子上。”
- **提供有限的选择**：当给予选择时，提供2-3个明确的选项，而不是开放式问题。例如：“你想先做数学作业，还是先做阅读作业？”而不是“你想做什么？”
- **允许延迟回应**：自闭症学生处理语言信息可能需要更长时间。提问后，等待至少5-10秒，让他们组织回应。不要重复提问或立即替他们回答。

### 3.3 差异化教学与任务设计

调整作业的难度和形式，以确保学生能体验到成功，从而提升参与动机。

- **任务分解**：将一个大型项目分解成若干个小步骤，每完成一步就给予积极的反馈和强化。
- **利用兴趣**：将学生的特殊兴趣（如恐龙、火车、数字）融入教学内容和例子中。例如，用火车车厢来教加法，用恐龙名来练习拼写。
- **提供多种表达方式**：允许学生通过绘画、打字、视频、口头报告或模型制作等多种方式展示他们的学习成果，不局限于书面作业。

> **关键事实来源**：IRIS中心（隶属于范德比尔特大学）强调，在差异化教学中，利用学生的兴趣和优势是提高自闭症学生参与度和积极性的有效策略 [4]。

## 4. 核心策略：社交与行为支持

### 4.1 正向行为干预与支持（PBIS）

PBIS的核心是“预防胜于纠正”。它强调通过明确期望、教授技能和积极强化来减少问题行为。

- **明确行为期望**：明确告诉学生“在课堂上，我们如何做？”（例如：双手放好、眼睛看老师、小嘴巴安静）。使用视觉海报展示这些规则。
- **高频率的积极强化**：不要只关注问题行为。当学生做出任何积极行为时（如看着老师、举手、安静地坐着），立即给予具体的表扬（“你真棒，我看你刚才非常专注地听讲”）或小奖励（如贴纸、额外时间）。
- **功能性行为评估（FBA）**：如果学生出现持续的挑战性行为，应进行FBA，找出行为背后的沟通目的（是为了逃避任务、获取关注、寻求感官刺激还是获得物品），然后设计替代行为教给学生。

> **关键事实来源**：美国教育部支持的PBIS技术援助中心指出，将PBIS框架应用于个别学生，特别是自闭症学生，对于改善其行为结果和学业参与度非常有效 [5]。

### 4.2 同伴中介介入（PMI）与社交技能训练

同伴可以成为强大的支持者和学习伙伴。

- **创建“友好伙伴”**：有意识地安排一位社交能力强的同伴，在小组活动、自由活动或课间帮助自闭症学生。该伙伴需要接受简单培训，如如何发起对话、如何邀请加入游戏。
- **结构化的社交小组**：在教师指导下，让几名自闭症学生和同伴一起进行社交游戏或活动，如轮流玩棋盘游戏、合作完成拼图。教师应在过程中提供即时反馈和指导。
- **视频示范**：让同伴或教师录制正确社交行为的视频（如如何打招呼、如何借东西），然后让自闭症学生观看和模仿。这是一种非常有效的、低压力的学习方式。

> **关键事实来源**：美国国家自闭症谱系障碍专业发展中心（NPDC）确认，同伴中介介入和视频示范均属于成熟的循证实践 [6]。

## 5. 总结与实施建议

增强自闭症学生的课堂参与度没有单一的“万能药”，其核心在于**个性化、结构化、可视化和正向强化**。有效的策略不是一次性干预，而是需要持续评估和调整的系统性方法。

**行动建议清单：**
1.  **评估优先**：使用简单的感官偏好清单或行为观察表，了解学生的具体需求。
2.  **从“环境”开始**：99%的问题源于环境不匹配。先调整教室的物理和感官环境。
3.  **建立信任**：与学生建立积极、尊重的关系。学生只有感到安全，才愿意参与。
4.  **与家长合作**：家长是了解孩子行为模式的最佳信息来源。定期沟通，保持策略的一致性。
5.  **小步快跑**：不要试图同时改变所有事情。选择一个或两个策略，坚持实施2-3周，评估效果，再进行调整和扩展。
6.  **教师自我关怀**：支持自闭症学生是一项情感劳动密集的工作。教师应寻求同事支持和专业培训，以保持自身的心理健康。

通过系统地应用上述策略，教育者可以将课堂从令人生畏的挑战场所，转变为让每位自闭症学生都能感到被接纳、被理解，并能够积极参与和茁壮成长的学习社区。

# 增强自闭症学生课堂参与度：深度研究报告

## 一、引言

自闭症谱系障碍（Autism Spectrum Disorder, ASD）学生因其独特的神经认知特征，在课堂环境中常常面临感官过载、社交沟通困难、执行功能挑战以及兴趣范围狭窄等问题。这些因素显著影响其课堂参与度，进而阻碍学业进步与社会融合。增强自闭症学生的课堂参与并不仅仅是“让他们安静坐着”，而是通过科学、系统、个性化的支持策略，帮助学生实现有意义的认知、社交与情感投入。本报告综合循证实践（Evidence-Based Practices, EBPs），从环境调整、教学策略、行为支持、社交参与及辅助技术五个维度，提供系统性的策略框架。

---

## 二、有效的策略分类与详细说明

### 2.1 物理环境与感官调整

自闭症学生普遍存在感官处理差异，教室环境中的光线、噪音、温度或视觉杂乱都可能成为参与障碍。

#### 2.1.1 提供感官友好型空间
- **关键策略**：设立“安静角”或感官休息区，配备降噪耳机、重力毯、可调节灯光等工具。允许学生在感到过度刺激时短暂离开集体活动区。
- **实证支持**：研究表明，提供感官休息区可减少挑战性行为高达40%，并显著提升后续任务参与度。
- **来源**：Autism Speaks, “Sensory-Friendly Classrooms”  
  https://www.autismspeaks.org/sensory-friendly-classrooms

#### 2.1.2 视觉结构与清晰边界
- **关键策略**：使用地面标记、桌椅分区、可视化日程表（如文字+图片）来明确每个区域的功能和一天的活动流程。TEACCH（自闭症与沟通障碍儿童的治疗与教育）方法中的“结构化教学”正是基于此原则。
- **实证支持**：TEACCH方法已被广泛验证能有效提升自闭症学生的独立性和任务完成率。
- **来源**：TEACCH Autism Program, University of North Carolina  
  https://www.teacch.com

### 2.2 教学策略与课程调整

#### 2.2.1 结构化教学与视觉支持
- **关键策略**：
  - **可视化日程表**：使用可移动的卡片或应用（如“Choiceworks”）展示“先做什么，后做什么”，降低对口头指令的依赖。
  - **任务分解（Task Analysis）**：将复杂任务分解为小步骤，并辅以图片或文字说明。
  - **工作系统**：明确告知学生“做什么、做多少、何时完成、下一步是什么”。
- **来源**：National Professional Development Center on Autism Spectrum Disorder (NPDC)  
  https://autismpdc.fpg.unc.edu/evidence-based-practices

#### 2.2.2 差异化教学与个性化调整
- **关键策略**：
  - **兴趣导向学习**：将学生的特殊兴趣（如火车、恐龙、数字）融入课程任务中。例如，用学生喜欢的动画角色制作数学应用题。
  - **选择权提供**：给予有限的选择，如“你想用铅笔还是马克笔写字？”或“先做数学还是先阅读？”选择权显著提升参与动机。
  - **多样化输出方式**：允许学生通过打字、画图、口述录音或展示模型等方式展示学习成果，而非仅限书面写作。
- **实证支持**：兴趣导向学习与提供选择权是循证实践中的核心动机策略。
- **来源**：IRIS Center, Vanderbilt University, “Providing Choices for Students with Autism”  
  https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/

#### 2.2.3 直接教学与明确期望
- **关键策略**：使用清晰、简洁、字面化的语言；避免讽刺、比喻或复杂的开放式问题。通过“示范-引导-独立”的脚手架模式进行教学。使用“先…然后…”的句式陈述期望。
- **来源**：AFIRM (Autism Focused Intervention Resources and Modules)  
  https://afirm.fpg.unc.edu/

### 2.3 行为支持与正向强化

#### 2.3.1 正向行为干预与支持（PBIS）
- **关键策略**：学校层面实施全校性PBIS，课堂层面使用差别强化（Differential Reinforcement），例如：
  - **DRA（替代行为强化）**：强化替代性适当行为，例如若学生试图打断，强化其举手行为。
  - **DRO（其他行为强化）**：在特定时间段内未出现目标问题行为时给予强化。
- **来源**：Center on PBIS  
  https://www.pbis.org/

#### 2.3.2 自我监控系统
- **关键策略**：教学生使用简单的自我记录表（如“我在听讲吗？”的勾选清单），自主评估自己的参与行为（如“眼睛看老师”、“手放好”、“回答问题”）。自我监控能有效提升任务专注度。
- **实证支持**：一项元分析显示自我监控对自闭症学生学业表现有中等至较大效应量。
- **来源**：Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders  
  https://link.springer.com/journal/10803

### 2.4 社交参与与同伴支持

#### 2.4.1 同伴介入策略（Peer-Mediated Instruction and Intervention, PMII）
- **关键策略**：培训典型发展同伴作为“同伴导师”，在小组活动、自由游戏或合作学习中有意识地引导自闭症学生参与。同伴导师提供示范、提示和正向反馈。
- **实证支持**：PMII是提升自闭症学生社交互动和课堂参与效率最高、自然度最高的策略之一。
- **来源**：NPDC, “Peer-Mediated Instruction and Intervention”  
  https://autismpdc.fpg.unc.edu/evidence-based-practices/peer-mediated-instruction-and-intervention

#### 2.4.2 社交叙事与视频示范
- **关键策略**：
  - **社交叙事（Social Stories™）**：由Carol Gray开发的简短、个性化故事，描述一个社交情境、期望行为和原因。例如，“上课时，当老师问问题，我可以举手。老师会叫我回答。”
  - **视频示范（Video Modeling）**：录制同龄人或成人展示正确参与行为（如排队、轮候发言、专注听讲）的视频，让学生反复观看并模仿。
- **实证支持**：视频示范对自闭症学生习得新行为具有一致的高效性。
- **来源**：Carol Gray Social Stories  
  https://carolgraysocialstories.com/  
  Indiana Resource Center for Autism, Video Modeling  
  https://www.iidc.indiana.edu/irca/

### 2.5 辅助技术（Assistive Technology, AT）

#### 2.5.1 低技术工具
- 可视化计时器（Time Timer）、降噪耳机、加权背心、沟通板（PECS）。

#### 2.5.2 高技术工具
- **沟通应用**：如Proloquo2Go、LAMP Words for Life，用于非口语或有限口语学生。
- **组织与任务管理应用**：如Choiceworks、First Then Visual Schedule、Todoist（简化版）。
- **专注与感官调节工具**：如Calm Counter、Breathe, Think, Do with Sesame。
- **来源**：Assistive Technology for Autism, Understood.org  
  https://www.understood.org/en/articles/assistive-technology-for-autism

---

## 三、实施建议与注意事项

1.  **个性化优先**：没有一种策略适用于所有自闭症学生。必须基于学生个体功能评估（如FBA、偏好评估）和IEP目标进行选择。
2.  **执行功能支持**：许多自闭症学生存在执行功能缺陷（计划、组织、时间管理）。将策略与执行功能训练结合，如使用“自我监控”和“任务分解”。
3.  **团队协作**：教师、特殊教育者、行为分析师（BCBA）、言语治疗师、家长需保持沟通一致，确保策略在课堂、家庭及其他环境中的一致性。
4.  **避免“一次性”使用**：策略需持续评估与调整。学生进步后，可逐步撤除支架（如提示、视觉支持），但需保留必要时可恢复的弹性。
5.  **文化敏感性与包容性**：在尊重学生家庭文化背景的前提下，选择适合的沟通方式和奖励系统。

---

## 四、总结

增强自闭症学生课堂参与度是一项系统工程，核心在于 **“理解神经多样性 + 提供个性化支持 + 创造包容环境”**。有效策略的共同特点是：**结构化、可视化、可预测、正向积极**。从环境感官调整到教学策略，从行为支持到社交融入，再到辅助技术的应用，每一条路径都指向同一个目标——让自闭症学生不仅“在场”，更真正“参与”并有意义地学习。

---

<answer>
# 增强自闭症学生课堂参与度的深度研究报告

## 1. 核心概念与背景

自闭症谱系障碍（Autism Spectrum Disorder, ASD）是一组以社交沟通障碍、兴趣狭窄和重复刻板行为为核心的神经发育障碍。在融合教育环境中，自闭症学生常面临感官超负荷、社交理解困难、语言表达障碍以及执行功能缺陷等挑战，导致课堂参与度显著低于同龄人。**课堂参与度** 不仅指学生是否在座位上听讲，更包括行为参与（完成任务、遵守规则）、认知参与（投入思考、解决问题）和情感参与（对学习感到兴趣、归属感）三个维度。研究表明，提升自闭症学生的课堂参与度，不仅能改善学业成绩，还能显著减少问题行为并增强社会适应能力。

---

## 2. 环境与结构策略

### 2.1 物理环境调整

- **视觉结构化**：利用图片、颜色编码、标签和日程表来明确区域功能。例如，在教室中设置“安静角”或“感官休息区”，用视觉提示说明每个区域的使用规则。研究表明，视觉结构能显著降低自闭症学生的焦虑水平，提高对课堂流程的预期能力。
- **感官友好设计**：减少荧光灯频闪（改用自然光或暖色灯），提供降噪耳机或可调节的座位（如摇椅、平衡球椅）。**感官过载**是自闭症学生课堂脱节的主要诱因之一，因此调整环境以降低刺激强度至关重要。
- **固定座位安排**：自闭症学生通常需要固定的座位以减少不确定性。座位应远离窗户、门和空调出风口等干扰源，并靠近教师以获取及时支持。

### 2.2 日程与过渡管理

- **可视化日程表**：使用图片或文字形式展示每日流程，每完成一项活动可让学生自行勾选或移除卡片。这有助于学生预测下一步，减少因过渡带来的焦虑。
- **提前预告变化**：如有特殊活动或日程变动，须提前15分钟、5分钟分别给予口头和视觉提示。例如使用“先—后”卡片（先完成数学，然后去操场）。

> **来源**：  
> - Hume, K., et al. (2021). *Evidence-Based Practices for Children, Youth, and Young Adults with Autism*. The University of North Carolina, Frank Porter Graham Child Development Institute. [https://ncaep.fpg.unc.edu/sites/ncaep.fpg.unc.edu/files/imce/documents/EBP%20Report%202020.pdf](https://ncaep.fpg.unc.edu/sites/ncaep.fpg.unc.edu/files/imce/documents/EBP%20Report%202020.pdf)  
> - 美国疾病控制与预防中心（CDC）：*Sensory Overload and Autism*. [https://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/autism/sensory.html](https://www.cdc.gov/ncbddd/autism/sensory.html)

---

## 3. 教学策略

### 3.1 差异化教学

- **任务分解**：将复杂任务拆解为小步骤，每完成一步给予即时强化。这符合自闭症学生常见的“中央统合弱”认知特点，即难以把握整体信息。
- **多模态呈现**：同时使用文字、图片、实物和口述讲解。例如，在讲解“光合作用”时，同时展示动画、示意图和实物叶片。
- **兴趣导向教学**：将学生的特殊兴趣（如火车、恐龙、编程）融入课程内容，作为增强物或教学载体。例如，用火车轨道讲解数学测量。

### 3.2 直接社交技能教学

- **社交故事**：由Carol Gray开发的社交故事（Social Stories™）通过描述特定社交情境，帮助学生理解他人期望和适当反应。例如，撰写一个关于“如何请求帮助”的社交故事，包括具体语句和步骤。
- **视频榜样**：播放同龄人正确展示目标行为（如课堂举手、排队）的视频，然后让学生模仿并回放录像以自我评估。
- **角色扮演**：在小组中设定场景，练习分享、轮流对话等技能。需注意，角色扮演应循序渐进，初期可从教师一对一示范开始。

### 3.3 增强与替代沟通（AAC）

- 对于非语言或语言表达能力有限的学生，使用图片交换沟通系统（PECS）、语音输出设备或平板电脑上的沟通应用。例如，学生可点击“我需要帮助”图标来发起互动，从而减少因无法表达而产生的挫败性行为。

> **来源**：  
> - Wong, C., et al. (2015). *Evidence-Based Practices for Children, Youth, and Young Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder*. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. [https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-014-2351-z](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10803-014-2351-z)  
> - 美国自闭症之声（Autism Speaks）：*Social Stories and Visual Supports*. [https://www.autismspeaks.org/tool-kit/atnair-p-social-stories-and-visual-supports](https://www.autismspeaks.org/tool-kit/atnair-p-social-stories-and-visual-supports)

---

## 4. 行为支持策略

### 4.1 正向行为干预与支持（PBIS）

- 学校应建立全校性的正向行为支持体系，明确期望行为（如“尊重、负责、安全”），并通过表扬、代币系统等方式强化积极行为。对自闭症学生应个性化调整，例如使用“选择菜单”（如“完成三项任务后可选择5分钟玩拼图”）。
- **功能性行为评估（FBA）** 是PBIS的关键步骤。通过分析问题行为的功能（如逃避任务、获取关注），设计替代行为教学。例如，若学生因任务难度而尖叫，则教其使用“我需要帮助”卡片。

### 4.2 自我监控

- 教授学生使用自我记录表，每完成一个学习环节后标记自己的参与状态（如“专注”或“走神”）。自我监控能提升学生对自身行为的觉察力，是提高课堂参与度的有效策略之一。

> **来源**：  
> - 美国教育部教育科学研究所（IES）What Works Clearinghouse：*Positive Behavioral Interventions and Supports (PBIS)*. [https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Intervention/103](https://ies.ed.gov/ncee/wwc/Intervention/103)  
> - 美国国家自闭症中心（NAC）：*National Standards Report, Phase 2*. [https://nationalautismcenter.org/national-standards-project/](https://nationalautismcenter.org/national-standards-project/)

---

## 5. 辅助技术应用

### 5.1 沟通与学习工具

- **语音生成设备（SGD）**：如iPad上的Proloquo2Go、LAMP Words for Life等应用，可用于非语言学生的课堂表达和提问。
- **任务管理应用**：如Choiceworks、First Then Visual Schedule，帮助自闭症学生管理时间与任务顺序。
- **文字转语音与语音转文字**：对于有书写障碍的学生，使用语音识别软件（如Dragon NaturallySpeaking）进行作业输入，减少书写负担。

### 5.2 感官调节工具

- 可穿戴设备（如智能手表）可设置定时提醒进行深呼吸或感官活动；提供可挤压的感官玩具（如应力球、弹力带）以帮助学生在课上释放多余能量。但需注意，这些工具应作为调节策略，而非分散注意力的玩具。

> **来源**：  
> - 自闭症技术协会（Autism Technology Association）：*Assistive Technology for Autism*. [https://www.autismtechnology.org/assistive-technology](https://www.autismtechnology.org/assistive-technology)  
> - 美国言语语言听力协会（ASHA）：*Augmentative and Alternative Communication (AAC)*. [https://www.asha.org/public/speech/disorders/AAC/](https://www.asha.org/public/speech/disorders/AAC/)

---

## 6. 社交与同伴互动策略

### 6.1 同伴支持

- **同伴导师制**：培训一名或多名友善的普通学生担任“同伴导师”，在课堂上辅助自闭症学生完成任务、参与讨论。同伴导师应接受关于自闭症特点的简单培训，并学会如何逐步引导而非直接给出答案。
- **社交小组**：在课内或课间引导自闭症学生与普通学生进行结构化游戏或合作学习，如拼图活动、科学实验小组。研究表明，结构化社交情境比自由互动更能促进自闭症学生的社交参与。

### 6.2 教师角色

- 教师应使用清晰的指令（如“请拿出蓝色笔记本，翻到第10页”）而非笼统表述（如“准备好上课”）。同时，给予自闭症学生**额外的等待时间**（至少5-10秒）以回应提问，避免因催促而中断其思考过程。

> **来源**：  
> - Kasari, C., et al. (2012). *Making the Connection: Randomized Controlled Trial of Social Skills Intervention for Young Children with Autism*. Journal of Child Psychology and Psychiatry. [https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-7610.2012.02551.x](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1469-7610.2012.02551.x)  
> - 英国自闭症协会（National Autistic Society）：*Supporting Social Interaction in the Classroom*. [https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/professional-practice/classroom-social-interaction](https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/professional-practice/classroom-social-interaction)

---

## 7. 家庭与学校合作

- 教师应与家长保持定期沟通，了解学生在家庭中的表现、兴趣变化以及感官敏感性细节。例如，若家长反馈学生因噪音而烦躁，教师可在学校提供降噪耳机。
- 共同制定**个别化教育计划（IEP）** 目标，确保家庭中的正向行为支持策略与学校一致。例如，家庭中使用代币系统，学校也采用相同系统以增强一致性。

> **来源**：  
> - 美国教育部特殊教育计划办公室（OSEP）：*Parent and Family Engagement in Special Education*. [https://sites.ed.gov/osep/](https://sites.ed.gov/osep/)  
> - 自闭症研究组织（Autism Research Institute）：*School-Home Collaboration*. [https://www.autism.org/school-home-collaboration/](https://www.autism.org/school-home-collaboration/)

---

## 8. 总结与建议

增强自闭症学生的课堂参与度是一个系统工程，需要**环境调整、教学优化、行为支持、技术辅助、同伴互动和家校合作**六方面协同努力。以下为关键行动要点：

| 策略领域 | 核心做法 | 预期效果 |
|---------|----------|----------|
| 环境与结构 | 视觉日程、感官友好区、固定座位 | 减少焦虑，提高可预测性 |
| 教学策略 | 任务分解、多模态呈现、兴趣导向 | 提升认知参与和任务完成率 |
| 行为支持 | PBIS、自我监控、FBA | 减少问题行为，增加积极行为 |
| 辅助技术 | AAC设备、任务管理应用 | 支持沟通与自我管理 |
| 社交互动 | 同伴导师、结构化社交小组 | 增强社交参与和归属感 |
| 家校合作 | IEP目标协同、定期沟通 | 确保策略一致性 |

**推荐优先级**：首先从**环境调整**和**视觉结构化**入手，因为这是成本最低、见效最快的策略。随后逐步引入**差异化教学**和**正向行为支持**。对于有沟通障碍的学生，应尽早评估并引入**AAC系统**。最后，**同伴导师制**和**家庭合作**是长期维持参与度的关键保障。

---

## 参考资料

<answer>
# 深度研究报告：增强自闭症学生课堂参与度的有效策略

## 摘要

自闭症谱系障碍（ASD）学生在课堂参与方面面临独特的挑战，包括感官敏感性、社交沟通障碍、执行功能困难以及对结构化环境的需求。本报告基于循证实践，系统梳理了增强自闭症学生课堂参与度的多维策略，涵盖环境调整、教学方法、社交支持、行为干预、技术辅助及家校合作六大领域。报告旨在为教育工作者、学校管理者及相关专业人员提供可操作的综合指导。

---

## 一、理解自闭症学生课堂参与面临的挑战

自闭症学生课堂参与度低通常并非源于缺乏学习意愿，而是由于以下障碍：

1. **感官过载**：教室中的灯光、噪音、气味等刺激可能导致过度敏感或低敏感反应，使学生难以集中注意力（National Autistic Society, 2024）。
2. **社交沟通困难**：难以理解非语言线索、社交规则及抽象指令，导致小组活动或集体讨论时感到孤立（American Psychiatric Association, 2022）。
3. **执行功能缺陷**：计划、组织、时间管理和任务切换能力较弱，影响完成多步骤任务的能力（Kenworthy et al., 2014）。
4. **对变化的抗拒**：对日常安排、教学流程或环境变化的适应困难，可能引发焦虑或行为问题（Bishop-Fitzpatrick et al., 2017）。

---

## 二、环境与感官调整策略

### 2.1 创建感官友好的教室环境

- **物理布局优化**：减少视觉杂乱，设置清晰的视觉边界（如地面标记、个人工作区），避免开放式座位安排（Center for Autism & Related Disabilities, 2023）。
- **感官调节区**：在教室角落设置“安静区”或“感官休息站”，配备降噪耳机、重力毯、软垫、安抚玩具等，供学生情绪或感官过载时使用（Los Angeles Unified School District, 2024）。
- **照明调整**：用自然光或暖色LED灯替代荧光灯，减少眩光；提供遮光板或太阳镜选项（Autism Speaks, 2024）。
- **噪音控制**：允许使用降噪耳机；在小组讨论时降低背景音量；提供“白噪音”机器（National Education Association, 2023）。

### 2.2 结构化教学与环境

- **视觉日程表**：使用图片或文字呈现每日课程流程，帮助学生预测活动变化，减少焦虑（Mesibov et al., 2005）。
- **任务可视化分解**：将复杂任务分解为步骤，以图示或清单形式呈现，增强可执行性（TEACCH Autism Program, 2024）。
- **个人化工作系统**：明确“做什么、做多少、何时完成、下一步做什么”，提升独立完成任务的能力（Hume et al., 2014）。

**来源**：
- National Autistic Society. (2024). *Sensory differences*. https://www.autism.org.uk/advice-and-guidance/topics/sensory-differences
- TEACCH Autism Program. (2024). *Structured Teaching*. https://teacch.com/structured-teaching/

---

## 三、教学与沟通策略

### 3.1 直接教学法

- **明确指令**：使用简洁、具体的语言，如“请打开课本第12页，阅读第二段并回答下面的问题”，而非“请大家认真阅读材料”（Wong et al., 2015）。
- **示范与建模**：教师或同伴展示期望行为的具体过程，如“像这样提出一个问题”（National Autism Center, 2015）。
- **正向反馈**：即时、具体地肯定学生的参与行为，如“你刚才举手回答问题的动作很好，谢谢你的分享”（Cooper et al., 2020）。

### 3.2 视觉支持系统

- **视觉提示卡**：用于课堂指令（如“安静”、“举手”）、社交脚本（如“如何加入对话”）和情绪表达（如“我需要休息”）（Rao & Gagie, 2006）。
- **图形组织器**：如思维导图、维恩图、流程图，帮助学生组织信息并理解概念关系（Browder et al., 2006）。

### 3.3 差异化教学

- **灵活评估方式**：允许学生通过口述、绘画、打字或选择式答题展示学习成果，而非仅限书面作业（Florida Department of Education, 2023）。
- **提供选择**：在任务难度、活动顺序或学习方式上给予选择空间，增强自主性和参与动机（Rispoli et al., 2013）。
- **强化兴趣**：将学生的特殊兴趣（如太空、恐龙、火车）融入课程内容，提升学习内在驱动力（Gunn & Delafield-Butt, 2016）。

**来源**：
- Wong, C., et al. (2015). *Evidence-Based Practices for Children, Youth, and Young Adults with Autism Spectrum Disorder*. Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s10803-014-2351-z
- National Autism Center. (2015). *Findings and Conclusions: National Standards Project, Phase 2*. https://nationalautismcenter.org/national-standards-project/

---

## 四、社交与同伴支持策略

### 4.1 同伴介入策略

- **同伴导师制**：培训一对一的同伴支持者，在课堂活动中提供社交提示、任务协助和情感支持（Bass & Mulick, 2007）。
- **小组合作结构化**：采用“合作学习”模式，为每位小组成员分配明确角色（如记录员、发言人），确保自闭症学生参与具体任务（Kamps et al., 2002）。

### 4.2 社交技能教学

- **社交故事**：编写简短故事描述特定社交情境及期望行为，帮助学生理解社交规则（Gray, 2010）。
- **视频示范**：播放正确社交互动的视频片段，让学生观察并模仿（Bellini & Akullian, 2007）。
- **角色扮演**：在安全环境中练习课堂讨论、提问、求助等社交技能（Leaf et al., 2016）。

**来源**：
- Gray, C. (2010). *The New Social Story Book*. Future Horizons. https://carolgraysocialstories.com/
- Bellini, S., & Akullian, J. (2007). *A Meta-Analysis of Video Modeling and Video Self-Modeling Interventions for Children and Adolescents with Autism Spectrum Disorders*. Exceptional Children. https://doi.org/10.1177/001440290707300401

---

## 五、行为管理与正向行为支持

### 5.1 功能性行为评估

- 在实施干预前，确定导致行为问题（如离开座位、拒绝参与）的潜在功能（逃避任务、获取注意、感官需求），并针对性设计替代行为（O'Neill et al., 2015）。

### 5.2 正向行为干预

- **代币制**：学生通过参与课堂活动获得代币，积累后可兑换偏好活动或奖励（Tarbox et al., 2006）。
- **行为契约**：与学生共同制定明确目标与奖励机制，增强自我管理能力（Cooper et al., 2020）。
- **情绪调节策略**：教授“冷静计划”如深呼吸、计数、请求暂停，并提供安全出口（Center on the Social and Emotional Foundations for Early Learning, 2024）。

**来源**：
- O'Neill, R. E., et al. (2015). *Functional Behavioral Assessment: A Practical Guide*. Pearson. https://www.pearson.com/store/p/functional-behavioral-assessment-a-practical-guide/P100000047000
- Center on the Social and Emotional Foundations for Early Learning. (2024). *Teaching Emotional Regulation*. https://csefel.vanderbilt.edu/

---

## 六、技术辅助策略

### 6.1 辅助沟通工具

- **图片交换沟通系统**：适用于非口语或口语有限的学生，通过图片交换表达需求与参与（Bondy & Frost, 2001）。
- **语音输出设备**：如平板电脑配合通信应用程序，帮助学生进行课堂口头参与（van der Meer & Rispoli, 2010）。

### 6.2 教育技术

- **交互式白板与应用程序**：使用视觉化、游戏化的学习软件（如Khan Academy Kids、Proloquo2Go）提升参与度（Fletcher-Watson, 2014）。
- **时间管理工具**：使用计时器或任务管理应用程序（如Timer+、Choiceworks）帮助学生完成时间分配与任务切换（Odom et al., 2015）。

**来源**：
- Bondy, A., & Frost, L. (2001). *The Picture Exchange Communication System*. Behavior Modification. https://doi.org/10.1177/0145445501252004
- van der Meer, L., & Rispoli, M. (2010). *Communication Interventions Involving Speech-Generating Devices for Children with Autism: A Review of the Literature*. Developmental Neurorehabilitation. https://doi.org/10.3109/17518423.2010.483368

---

## 七、家校合作与教师支持

### 7.1 家校协作

- **定期沟通**：建立家校日志或数字化沟通平台，互通学生在校与在家的表现、策略与需求（Henderson & Mapp, 2002）。
- **共同制定个别化教育计划**：确保家长参与目标设定与策略设计，提升一致性（Turnbull et al., 2015）。
- **家庭延伸训练**：将课堂策略（如视觉日程表、社交故事）延伸至家庭环境，强化学习效果（Matson et al., 2009）。

### 7.2 教师专业发展

- **持续培训**：提供关于自闭症特征、循证教学策略、行为管理及感官支持的培训（National Professional Development Center on ASD, 2024）。
- **同伴支持**：建立校内或区域自闭症教师支持小组，共享经验与资源（Bene et al., 2014）。

**来源**：
- National Professional Development Center on ASD. (2024). *Professional Development Modules*. https://ncpd.unc.edu/autism
- Turnbull, A., et al. (2015). *Exceptional Lives: Special Education in Today's Schools*. Pearson.

---

## 八、关键建议与实施框架

### 8.1 实施建议

1. **个性化优先**：每位自闭症学生的需求与优势不同，策略应基于个别化评估（如IEP）设计。
2. **循序渐进**：从单一策略入手，逐步集成多项干预，避免学生因过多变化而感到压力。
3. **数据驱动**：定期收集学生参与度数据（如时长、次数、质量），评估干预效果并调整。
4. **包容性文化**：全校范围内推广神经多样性友好理念，减少污名化与偏见。

### 8.2 实施框架示例

| 阶段 | 目标 | 行动示例 |
|------|------|----------|
| 评估 | 了解学生需求与优势 | 功能性行为评估、感官偏好问卷 |
| 设计 | 制定个性化支持计划 | 视觉日程表、任务分解、代币制 |
| 实施 | 在课堂中执行策略 | 教师培训、同伴导师培训 |
| 监测 | 评估参与度变化 | 每周行为记录、师生反馈 |
| 调整 | 根据数据优化方案 | 修改奖励机制、增加感官调节时间 |

---

## 九、结论

增强自闭症学生的课堂参与度是一项系统工程，需要教育工作者、学校管理者、家长及专业人员的协同努力。通过环境优化、教学调整、社交支持、行为干预、技术辅助及家校合作六大策略的综合运用，绝大多数自闭症学生能够实现更高水平的课堂参与，从而获得更好的学业与社交成果。关键原则是：**尊重个体差异、基于循证实践、持续评估与调整、营造包容氛围**。

## 「全校參與分層支援有自閉症的學生」計劃

教育局於二○一一／一二學年開始，分階段在主流中小學推行加強支援有自閉症的學生的先導計劃，旨在發展出一套既適用於本地學校又具成效的「全校參與分層支援有自閉症的學生」三層支援模式 (「分層支援自閉症」模式)，通過運用有實證支持的策略，協助學生發展學習、社交和情緒方面的適應能力，促進他們有效地融入課堂學習及社群。有見先導計劃的成果顯著，教育局由二○二○／二一學年起將這項計劃恆常化。

在分層支援自閉症模式下，學校運用三個層次具針對性及實證的策略，支援有自閉症的學生，包括推行第一層全校性的策略，優化課堂教學，以營造自閉症友善的環境，例如運用視覺策略及流程表、有系統的常規、清晰的要求及簡單而明確的指示等，讓有自閉症的學生能明白及有效地參與課堂活動；在第二層支援方面，學校為有需要的學生提供額外的小組訓練，以提升他們的社交溝通、情緒適應及學習適應等技巧及能力；而在第三層支援方面，學校會為面對較大適應困難有自閉症的學生安排橫跨三層的個別學習計劃。 [...] ##### I.社會適應技巧小組訓練

為加強第二層支援的效能，教育局繼續採用「賽馬會喜伴同行：自閉症支援計劃」證實有效的學校與非政府機構協作模式，以非政府機構支援有自閉症的學生的專長，協助學校安排「分層支援自閉症」模式下的第二層支援，即額外社會適應技巧小組訓練。非政府機構的專業人員會根據組內學生的特殊需要，設計及執行各項訓練，提升各人的社交認知、人際溝通、情緒管理和學習等技巧，幫助他們在學習和社交適應上更順利地融入學校、家庭及社區的生活。

同時，學校人員透過從旁觀摩和參與小組訓練活動，把小組中有效的策略運用到課堂，幫助學生將在小組學到的技巧應用到真實的課堂及情境，提升其學習效能。計劃亦為相關家長及教師提供諮詢服務，加強各人照顧有自閉症的學生的專業知識及能力。

##### II. 強項為本小組 [...] 為促進學校運用「分層支援自閉症」模式，「全校參與分層支援有自閉症的學生計劃」透過「跨專業到校支援」及「學校與非政府協作」兩大部分，協助學校有系統地掌握該模式及其相關策略，以支援校內有自閉症的學生。

#### 第一部分：跨專業到校支援

在計劃的第一部分，教育局的教育心理學家及計劃人員組成的團隊會為教師提供情境學習和實踐為本的引導 (practice-based coaching)，通過諮商、個案討論、觀課及回饋、舉辦工作坊和聯校網絡交流等活動，提升學校人員支援有自閉症的學生的信心及能力，落實推行三層支援模式及相關策略。

## 4. 管理过渡和变化

过渡通常是自闭症学生面临的困难时刻，因为他们需要可预见性，并且在处理变化时存在困难。这些从一种活动过渡到另一种活动的时刻，如果没有提前预见和准备，可能会产生压力和不当行为。

预见是成功过渡的关键。提前几分钟通知学生即将发生的变化，使用具体的时间标记：“在 5 分钟内，我们将收拾书本去休息。”使用视觉或听觉计时器来具体化剩余时间，这有助于学生在心理上为变化做好准备。

建立清晰且一致的过渡例程。例如，从个人工作转到小组活动时，定义一个明确的顺序：收拾材料、合上书本、起身、推开椅子、走向小组活动区域。这种仪式化使学生感到安心，并逐步自动化预期的行为。

[摘 要] 随着融合教育理念逐渐深入人心，自闭症学生在普通学校中的数量逐年增多，如何在 学校课堂和校园生活中，有效干预学生的不良行为，帮助学生更好的适应社会及成长，这是教 育的难题和课题。通过文献与案例的分析整理，阐述自闭症学生在融合教育背景下的多样化行 为干预策略的实践，文章主要从融合教育和自闭症学生自身的行为特点进行梳理行为干预的理 论依据，并结合具体的教学情况，对不同类型的多样化干预策略在不同的教学环节及生活情景 中所产生的作用进行分析。通过研究得知，结构化教学、积极行为支持、同伴互助、情绪调节 训练等策略的混合运用，可明显优化自闭症学生的各种行为表现以及学习参与度，在提升其社 会交往能力和情绪管理方面也存在积极影响。笔者给出在融合教育里开展行为干预的可持续发 展意见，希望给一线教师和学校管理者给予可供参考的想法。

Diversified Practices of Behavioral Intervention Strategies for Autistic Students in Inclusive Education 

Yuansheng Guo Special Education School of Guangshan County, Henan Province 

Abstract: As the concept of inclusive education gradually takes root in people's hearts, the number of autistic students in regular schools is increasing year by year. How to effectively intervene in students' bad behaviors in school classrooms and campus life, and help students better adapt to society and grow, is a difficult problem and topic in education. Through the analysis and organization of literature and cases, this article expounds the practice of diversified behavioral intervention strategies for students with autism in the context of inclusive education. The article mainly sorts out the theoretical basis of behavioral intervention from the perspectives of inclusive education and the behavioral characteristics of students with autism themselves, and combines specific teaching situations. Analyze the effects of different types of diversified intervention strategies in various teaching links and life scenarios. Through research, it has been found that the combined application of strategies such as structured teaching, positive behavior support, peer assistance, and emotional regulation training can significantly optimize the various behavioral performances and learning participation of students with autism, and also has a positive impact on improving their social interaction skills and emotional management. The author offers sustainable development suggestions for behavioral intervention in inclusive education, hoping to provide reference ideas for front-line teachers and school administrators.

引言 

> 融合教育属于现代教育重要理念，重视尊重学生个体差 异，提倡把有特殊教育需求的学生融入普通教育体系之中， 在平等，包容的环境里共同学习，成长，自闭症学生的教育 需求较为突出，自闭症谱系障碍学生在社交，沟通，兴趣， 行为模式等方面存在差异，常常表现出刻板行为，情绪波动 以及适应困难等现象，如果这些行为特征没有得到妥善处理， 就会影响到自闭症学生的课堂参与度，同伴交往情况以及学 业成绩提升状况，同样也会影响到班级整体的教学秩序。 但是融合教育情境下行为干预比传统特殊教育环境更 具挑战性，普通课堂节奏快、学生人数多、教学任务重，教 师要在有限时间内兼顾所有学生的学习进度和特殊学生的 个别化需求，这就要求教育者不仅要掌握特殊教育专业知识， 还要灵活运用各种干预策略，将干预策略自然融入课堂和校

# 教育研究         

> 第8卷◆第 11 期◆版本 1.0 ◆2025 年文章类型：论文 |刊号（ ISSN ）： 2630-4686 / （中图刊号）： 380GL020

## Education Research 

11 

园活动之中，保证干预有效且持续。本文意在探索融合教育 环境里自闭症学生行为干预策略的多样化实施路径，分析不 同策略在实际操作中的优缺点并给出改善意见，从而给教育 实践给予理论和经验支撑。 

1 融合教育下自闭症学生行为干预的理论基础 

1.1 融合教育理念与发展趋向 融合教育的核心理念是“教育公平”与“个性发展”， 主张在普通教育环境中接纳和支持所有的学生，包括那些具 有特殊教育需求的学生，这不仅是教育模式的创新，更是社 会价值观的体现，它强调的是通过提供平等的学习机会，让 每一个学生在共同体中发挥最大的潜能。国际上，融合教育 的理念起源于 20 世纪末特殊教育向普通教育体系的融入运 动，以 1994 年联合国教科文组织发布的《萨拉曼卡宣言》 为标志，明确提出“普通学校应该接纳所有儿童，不论他们 身体、智力、社会情感、语言或其他条件存在何种差异”， 此后，美国《残疾人教育法案》（ IDEA ）和英国《特殊教 育需求与残疾法案》（ SEND ）等立法也陆续确立了融合教 育的法律地位。 在我国， 融合教育的发展与“随班就读” 政策密切相关， 

20 世纪 80 年代末到 90 年代初， 教育部开展了大规模的随班 就读试点，逐渐形成了普通学校为主导、特殊教育学校为辅 助的特殊教育体系，进入 21 世纪以来，《残疾人教育条例》 《特殊教育提升计划（ 2014-2016 ）》和之后的《特殊教育提 升计划（ 2017-2020 ）》陆续出台，提出扩大随班就读规模、 加强教师培训、改善资源教室条件等一系列措施，这些政策 推动融合教育在城乡各地迅速发展，普通学校接纳自闭症学 生的数量也随之增多 [1] 。不过，理念落地不是那么顺利，融合教育在我国发展存 在“快与慢”并存的情况，一方面政策推动和公众认知改善 给自闭症学生融入普通学校创造了机会，另一方面教师素质、 学校资源分配和社会支持体系的不足阻碍了融合教育深入 展开， 对于自闭症学生来说， 进入普通课堂不代表真正融入， 重点是学校能否在课程安排、教学方法和行为管理上给予恰 当支持。在融合教育里，行为干预是支持自闭症学生的重要 方式，也是维持课堂秩序，保证其他学生学习权利的重要手 段，有效的干预应该遵循尊重，包容和科学的原则，注重在 自然环境里促进技能掌握和行为改进，还要符合学生的个人 发展需求。 

1.2 自闭症学生行为特征及干预需求分析 自闭症学生的行为方面表现差别挺大，不过大致包含四 大部分，那就是社会交往障碍，兴趣窄小，刻板重复行为， 感官异常，这几个特征会在不同年龄段以及不同的状况之下 显现出来，就拿低年级的小学来说，有些孩子也许会常常在 课堂上离开座位，发出一些和授课内容没有关系的声音，或 者突然遭遇环境上的改变就情绪大乱，再比如说高年级学生， 可能会出现拒绝合作学习的情况，而且小组讨论时也缄默不 发一言，更过分的话还会极力避开同伴身体上的碰触 [2] 。

1.3 行为干预的理论依据 融合教育中的行为干预策略主要是基于多个理论基础 之上，其中最主要的有应用行为分析，积极行为支持以及社 会学习理论。 ABA 是行为干预的方法，是根据实证，明确行 为目标，分析行为功能，设计环境调整和强化计划，改变学 生行为。 比如对于课堂打断行为， ABA 会先通过功能性行为 评估， 确定行为的目的 （寻求关注、 逃避任务、 感官刺激等） ，然后通过减少触发因素、教授替代行为、给予正强化等方式 逐步减少问题行为。 ABA 的优点是可以测量、可以复制，但 是需要与自然的教学情境相结合，在融合教育中，不能过于 “训练化”，要让学生有参与课堂的感觉 [3] 。

PBS 是在 ABA 的基础之上发展起来的，更强调的则是 环境的优化和支持。认为行为问题的发生跟环境的状况以及 学生的技能都有很大的关系。所以干预不单单是针对行为进 行干预，还要改善能够导致这些问题发生的环境状况，并且 给予学生所需要的一些技能训练。 

2 融合教育中自闭症学生行为干预的多样化实践 策略 

2.1 结构化教学策略 结构化教学是自闭症学生普遍采用的干预手段，它强调 的是通过环境的布置，任务的视觉指示以及日常的流程来减 少学生因为不确定性带来的不安和行为问题。在融合教育中， 教师可以在教室里划分出学习区和活动区，通过图片、时间 表或者任务卡清楚地告诉学生需要学习什么以及要做什么， 这样可以帮助学生建立起对于课堂节奏的预期，减少课堂中 离座和分心的行为，提高学生对任务的持续关注。教师在实 施的过程中要保持指令的简洁，重复适当，同时根据学生的 兴趣选择教学材料，以此提高学生参与的积极性 [4] 。

2.2 积极行为支持策略 积极行为支持注重分析行为背后的功能，改变引发问题 行为的环境因素，并利用强化来培养替代的积极行为，在融 合教育环境中，教师可先通过观察与记录找出问题行为的诱 因及其后果，然后规划替代行为的教学及强化方案，拿那些 由于任务太难就经常逃避的学生来说，教师可以先削减任务 要求，慢慢加大难度，当学生完成任务之后，立刻予以赞扬 或者奖励，如此一来，既能削减问题行为，又能加强学生的 自我效能感和学习动力，而且，积极行为支持十分看重和家 庭的合作，让干预策略在学校和家庭中得以统一，进而提升 干预的稳定性和持久性。 教育研究         

> 第8卷◆第 11 期◆版本 1.0 ◆2025 年文章类型：论文 |刊号（ ISSN ）： 2630-4686 / （中图刊号）： 380GL020

Copyright © This work is licensed under a Commons Attibution-Non Commercial 4.0 International License. 

## Education Research 

12 2.3 同伴互助策略 同伴互助属于融合教育里特有的且有效的干预手段之 一，通过促使普通学生充当“学习伙伴”或者“社交伙伴” ，自闭症学生就能在平日交流时学会社会交往准则和恰当的 行为表现，譬如在小组合作活动当中，教师可以安排一个耐 性好而且乐于助人的同学和自闭症学生成对，一同去完成任 务，期间给予及时提示和鼓舞，同伴互助有益于缩减孤立和 退缩行为，而且可以加强自闭症学生的自信心以及社会适应 水平，而且能够推动普通学生的同理心和包容度，营造互助 友好的班级环境。 

2.4 情绪调节训练策略 情绪调节困难是自闭症学生出现冲动或者攻击性行为 的关键原因，情绪调节训练要让学生学会识别自己的情绪状 况，还要学会恰当地表达和缓解情绪的方式，在融合教育环 境里，教师可以利用可视化工具，像情绪卡片或者情绪温度 计，帮助学生用非语言手段表达自己的情绪，而且，教师还 可以做情景模拟或者角色扮演之类的训练，让学生学会在遇 到挫折或者冲突的时候怎么应对，教师可以设立一个“冷静 角”，当学生情绪高涨的时候，他们可以暂时离开教室，以 免发生冲突，经过长时间的训练，学生慢慢学会了自己调节 情绪的办法， 这样就能减少因为情绪失控引发的行为问题 [5] 。

3 融合教育中多样化干预策略的综合应用与效果 研究 

3.1 策略整合的必要性 融合教育里，单一策略很难应付自闭症学生的种种需求， 学生的行为问题也许牵扯到环境适应，情绪调节，社交互动 等诸多方面，所以要把结构化教学，积极行为支撑，同伴互 助以及情绪调节训练这些策略综合起来，拿课堂来说，教师 既可以凭借结构化安排给予可预期的环境，又可以把积极行 为支撑机制同积极表现联系起来，而且通过同伴互助增进社 会交往，必要时还能做情绪调节引导，这样一来，这些策略 就能从多个层面同步起作用，从而明显改善干预的总体成效。 

3.2 实践效果与案例分析 一些融合教育试点学校中，多样化的干预手段综合使用 后收获了较好的成果，有一个三年级自闭症孩子，经过结构 化教学与积极行为支持之后，课堂上离座行为明显变少，任 务完成率从 40% 升到 85% 以上， 而且同伴互助使他参加小组 讨论的次数和质量都得到改善，在另一个事例里，情绪调节 训练让一个情绪起伏很大的孩子懂得当生气的时候用深呼 吸和 “冷静角”的办法来化解情绪， 这样就免去好几次冲突。 

4 融合教育中行为干预策略的实施挑战与优化建议 

4.1 面临的主要挑战 融合教育里行为干预的实际操作，还是存在很多难题。 一方面，普通教师对特殊教育知识和技能准备不充分，造成 策略执行的专业性欠缺，另一方面，班上学生太多，课时太 紧，老师在课堂上很难做到针对个别学生进行干预又照顾到 整体教学，学校跟家庭之间的交流也不顺畅，这同样会影响 到干预的效果和一致性，缺乏足够资源，教师培训制度不完 善等情况，也限制着这些干预策略的全面推行。 

4.2 改进与发展建议 要想改良融合教育里自闭症学生的行为干预效果，就要 从很多方面加以改善，要加大教师培训力度，保证教师懂得 应用行为分析，积极行为支持这些关键方法，而且能够依照 学生的不同之处灵活调整，要改良班级构成，适当地缩减班 额或者增添助教，这样可以提升教师开展个别化干预的可能 性， 第三， 创建家校协作机制， 保证学校和家庭在干预目的， 方法和奖励机制方面达成统一，要强化政策和资源方面的支 撑， 给予专门的教具， 情绪调节工具， 而且给教师参加研修， 交流等活动给予条件，从而促使各种策略得以可持续发展。 

5 结论 

融合教育给自闭症学生赋予了公平参与并全面发展的 机遇，不过，它的有效与否取决于科学且灵活的行为干预策 略，本文所探究的结构化教学，积极行为支撑，同伴互助以 及情绪调节练习等众多操作，可以在不同层面上符合自闭症 学生的需求，而且，在这些干预手段综合运用时会产生叠加 效果，日后，应该加大对教师培训及资源保障的力度，增进 家校协作，促使干预策略在融合教育当中不断改进并得到推 广，只有这样，融合教育才可能真正发挥出价值，从而让自 闭症学生在尊重与支持之下发挥自己的潜能。

  "evidence": "2 融合教育中自闭症学生行为干预的多样化实践策略

2.1 结构化教学策略
结构化教学是自闭症学生普遍采用的干预手段，它强调的是通过环境的布置，任务的视觉指示以及日常的流程来减少学生因为不确定性带来的不安和行为问题。在融合教育中，教师可以在教室里划分出学习区和活动区，通过图片、时间表或者任务卡清楚地告诉学生需要学习什么以及要做什么，这样可以帮助学生建立起对于课堂节奏的预期，减少课堂中离座和分心的行为，提高学生对任务的持续关注。教师在实施的过程中要保持指令的简洁，重复适当，同时根据学生的兴趣选择教学材料，以此提高学生参与的积极性 [4]。

2.2 积极行为支持策略
积极行为支持注重分析行为背后的功能，改变引发问题行为的环境因素，并利用强化来培养替代的积极行为，在融合教育环境中，教师可先通过观察与记录找出问题行为的诱因及其后果，然后规划替代行为的教学及强化方案，拿那些由于任务太难就经常逃避的学生来说，教师可以先削减任务要求，慢慢加大难度，当学生完成任务之后，立刻予以赞扬或者奖励，如此一来，既能削减问题行为，又能加强学生的自我效能感和学习动力，而且，积极行为支持十分看重和家庭的合作，让干预策略在学校和家庭中得以统一，进而提升干预的稳定性和持久性。

2.3 同伴互助策略
同伴互助属于融合教育里特有的且有效的干预手段之一，通过促使普通学生充当“学习伙伴”或者“社交伙伴”，自闭症学生就能在平日交流时学会社会交往准则和恰当的行为表现，譬如在小组合作活动当中，教师可以安排一个耐性好而且乐于助人的同学和自闭症学生成对，一同去完成任务，期间给予及时提示和鼓舞，同伴互助有益于缩减孤立和退缩行为，而且可以加强自闭症学生的自信心以及社会适应水平，而且能够推动普通学生的同理心和包容度，营造互助友好的班级环境。

2.4 情绪调节训练策略
情绪调节困难是自闭症学生出现冲动或者攻击性行为的关键原因，情绪调节训练要让学生学会识别自己的情绪状况，还要学会恰当地表达和缓解情绪的方式，在融合教育环境里，教师可以利用可视化工具，像情绪卡片或者情绪温度计，帮助学生用非语言手段表达自己的情绪，而且，教师还可以做情景模拟或者角色扮演之类的训练，让学生学会在遇到挫折或者冲突的时候怎么应对，教师可以设立一个“冷静角”，当学生情绪高涨的时候，他们可以暂时离开教室，以免发生冲突，经过长时间的训练，学生慢慢学会了自己调节情绪的办法，这样就能减少因为情绪失控引发的行为问题 [5]。

3 融合教育中多样化干预策略的综合应用与效果研究

3.1 策略整合的必要性
融合教育里，单一策略很难应付自闭症学生的种种需求，学生的行为问题也许牵扯到环境适应，情绪调节，社交互动等诸多方面，所以要把结构化教学，积极行为支撑，同伴互助以及情绪调节训练这些策略综合起来，拿课堂来说，教师既可以凭借结构化安排给予可预期的环境，又可以把积极行为支撑机制同积极表现联系起来，而且通过同伴互助增进社会交往，必要时还能做情绪调节引导，这样一来，这些策略就能从多个层面同步起作用，从而明显改善干预的总体成效。

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Page 2: Evidence-Based Practices

URL Source: https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/cresource/q1/p02

Markdown Content:
## What do educators need to know about EBPs for children with autism?

To improve the outcomes of children with ASD, educators should implement [evidence-based practices (EBPs)](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/cresource/q1/javascript_required.html), strategies that have been shown to be effective in teaching appropriate behaviors and skills and decreasing inappropriate behaviors for a given population. There are evidence-based practices to improve academic and behavior outcomes for all students. However, this module will focus on strategies that have been shown to be effective in teaching appropriate behaviors and skills and decreasing inappropriate behaviors for students with ASD. The National Professional Development Center (NPDC) on Autism Spectrum Disorder has identified 27 evidence-based practices for improving outcomes for students with ASD.

EBP Definition
**Antecedent-based intervention**Arrangement of events or circumstances that precede the occurrence of an interfering behavior and designed to lead to the reduction of the behavior.
**Cognitive behavioral intervention**Instruction on management or control of cognitive processes that lead to changes in overt behavior.
**Differential reinforcement of alternative, incompatible, or other behavior**Provision of positive/desirable consequences for behaviors or their absence that reduce the occurrence of an undesirable behavior. Reinforcement provided: a) when the learner is engaging in a specific desired behavior other than the inappropriate behavior (DRA), b) when the learner is engaging in a behavior that is physically impossible to do while exhibiting the inappropriate behavior (DRI), or c) when the learner is not engaging in the interfering behavior (DRO).
**Discrete trial teaching**Instructional process usually involving one teacher/service provider and one student/client and designed to teach appropriate behavior or skills. Instruction usually involves massed trials. Each trial consists of the teacher’s instruction/presentation, the child’s response, a carefully planned consequence, and a pause prior to presenting the next instruction.
**Exercise**Increase in physical exertion as a means of reducing problem behaviors or increasing appropriate behavior.
**Extinction**Withdrawal or removal of reinforcers of interfering behavior in order to reduce the occurrence of that behavior. Although sometimes used as a single intervention practice, extinction often occurs in combination with functional behavior assessment, functional communication training, and differential reinforcement.
**Functional behavior assessment (FBA)**Systematic collection of information about an interfering behavior designed to identify functional contingencies that support the behavior. FBA consists of describing the interfering or problem behavior, identifying antecedent or consequent events that control the behavior, developing a hypothesis of the function of the behavior, and/or testing the hypothesis.
**Functional communication training**Replacement of interfering behavior that has a communication function with more appropriate communication that accomplishes the same function. Functional communication training usually includes FBA, differential reinforcement of alternative behavior, and/ or extinction.
**Modeling**Demonstration of a desired target behavior that results in imitation of the behavior by the learner and that leads to the acquisition of the imitated behavior. This EBP is often combined with other strategies such as prompting and reinforcement.
**Naturalistic intervention**Intervention strategies that occur within the typical setting/activities/routines in which the learner participates. Teachers/service providers establish the learner’s interest in a learning event through arrangement of the setting/activity/routine, provide necessary support for the learner to engage in the targeted behavior, elaborate on the behavior when it occurs, and/or arrange natural consequences for the targeted behavior or skills.
**Parent-implemented intervention**Parents provide individualized intervention to their child to improve/increase a wide variety of skills and/or to reduce interfering behaviors. Parents learn to deliver interventions in their home and/or community through a structured parent training program.
**Peer-mediated instruction and intervention**Typically developing peers interact with and/or help children and youth with ASD to acquire new behavior, communication, and social skills by increasing social and learning opportunities within natural environments. Teachers/service providers systematically teach peers strategies for engaging children and youth with ASD in positive and extended social interactions in both teacher-directed and learner-initiated activities.
**Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS)**Learners are initially taught to give a picture of a desired item to a communicative partner in exchange for the desired item. PECS consists of six phases which are: (1) “how” to communicate, (2) distance and persistence, (3) picture discrimination, (4) sentence structure, (5) responsive requesting, and (6) commenting.
**Pivotal response training**Pivotal learning variables (i .e., motivation, responding to multiple cues, self-management, and self-initiations) guide intervention practices that are implemented in settings that build on learner interests and initiative.
**Prompting**Verbal, gestural, or physical assistance given to learners to assist them in acquiring or engaging in a targeted behavior or skill. Prompts are generally given by an adult or peer before or as a learner attempts to use a skill.
**Reinforcement**An event, activity, or other circumstance occurring after a learner engages in a desired behavior that leads to the increased occurrence of the behavior in the future.
**Response interruption/ redirection**Introduction of a prompt, comment, or other distracters when an interfering behavior is occurring that is designed to divert the learner’s attention away from the interfering behavior and results in its reduction.
**Scripting**A verbal and/or written description about a specific skill or situation that serves as a model for the learner. Scripts are usually practiced repeatedly before the skill is used in the actual situation
**Self-management**Instruction focusing on learners discriminating between appropriate and inappropriate behaviors, accurately monitoring and recording their own behaviors, and rewarding themselves for behaving appropriately.
**Social narratives**Narratives that describe social situations in some detail by highlighting relevant cues and offering examples of appropriate responding. Social narratives are individualized according to learner needs and typically are quite short, perhaps including pictures or other visual aids.
**Social skills training**Group or individual instruction designed to teach learners with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) ways to appropriately interact with peers, adults, and other individuals. Most social skill meetings include instruction on basic concepts, role-playing or practice, and feedback to help learners with ASD acquire and practice communication, play, or social skills to promote positive interactions with peers.
**Structured play group**Small group activities characterized by their occurrences in a defined area and with a defined activity, the specific selection of typically developing peers to be in the group, a clear delineation of theme and roles by adult leading, prompting, or scaffolding as needed to support students’ performance related to the goals of the activity.
**Task analysis**A process in which an activity or behavior is divided into small, manageable steps in order to assess and teach the skill. Other practices, such as reinforcement, video modeling, or time delay, are often used to facilitate acquisition of the smaller steps.
**Technology-aided instruction and intervention (TAII)**Instruction or interventions in which technology (e.g., tablet, computer, computer program, online activity) is used to increase or maintain functional skills and behaviors.
**Time delay**In a setting or activity in which a learner should engage in a behavior or skill, a brief delay occurs between the opportunity to use the skill and any additional instructions or prompts. The purpose of the time delay is to allow the learner to respond without having to receive a prompt and thus focuses on fading the use of prompts during instructional activities .
**Video modeling**A visual model of the targeted behavior or skill (typically in the behavior, communication, play, or social domains), provided via video recording and display equipment to assist learning in or engaging in a desired behavior or skill .
**Visual support**Any visual display that supports the learner engaging in a desired behavior or skills independent of prompts. Examples of visual supports include pictures, written words, objects within the environment, arrangement of the environment or visual boundaries, schedules, maps, labels, organization systems, and timelines.

Adapted from Wong, Odom, Hume, Cox, Fettig, Kucharczyk, Brock, Plavnick, Fleury & Schultz, 2014. Retrieved from https://autismpdc.fpg.unc.edu/sites/autismpdc.fpg.unc.edu/files/imce/documents/table7_working_definition_ebp.pdf

[Click here to download and save a PDF version of the list](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/wp-content/uploads/modules/asd2/pdf/asd2_27ebp_definitions.pdf#content).

With so many EBPs from which to choose, how can educators or practitioners determine which of them to use with a specific child? The four steps outlined below can help educators and practitioners make a more informed decision when they select an EBP.

The _target behavior_ is the behavior the teacher wants to change. This should be a discrete behavior that is directly observable, measurable, and clearly defined. The definition of the behavior should:

*   Describe the behavior in an observable manner
*   Describe the behavior in measurable terms (i.e., instances of the behavior can be counted or timed)
*   Identify the setting in which the behavior occurs

Note the difference in the definitions below.

1.   Ambiguous and subjective definition: _Michelle violates other’s personal space_.
2.   Clear and observable definition: _When talking to someone, Michelle stands within a foot of that person_.

Defining behavior in this manner allows multiple professionals to observe and collect objective data on the behavior. If multiple professionals gather data using the second definition of Michelle’s behavior, they are more likely to collect data on the same behavior rather than on their subjective opinion of personal space violation.

To learn more about how to clearly define a student’s behavior so that when it occurs it can be reliably identified, measured, or counted, visit the following IRIS Case Study:

*   [Defining Behavior](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/wp-content/uploads/pdf_case_studies/ics_defbeh.pdf#content)

_Baseline data_ refers to the level (i.e., frequency, duration) at which a behavior occurs before a strategy or intervention is implemented. These data should be gathered for at least four days or until a pattern of behavior is evident. By comparing these data to data collected after the strategy has been implemented, educators can determine whether it is effective for the student.

To learn more about collecting observational data on a child or student’s behavior, visit the following IRIS Case Study:

*   [Measuring Behavior](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/wp-content/uploads/pdf_case_studies/ics_measbeh.pdf#content)

Once the target behavior has been identified and baseline data collected, the goal needs to be indicated in a child’s [individualized education program (IEP)](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/cresource/q1/javascript_required.html) or [individualized family service plan (IFSP)](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/cresource/q1/javascript_required.html). The goal should include information about:

*   When or where the behavior will be performed
*   What behavior should be displayed
*   Specific, measurable criterion for mastery

Note the difference in the goals below.

1.   Poorly written goal: _Michelle will respect other’s personal space_.
2.   Observable goal: _When talking to friends or school personnel, Michelle will stand a minimum of 1½ feet from them at least 90% of the time_.

The next step in this process is to determine which EBPs can address the target behavior. With those in mind, educators can select an EBP that is likely to be effective for a student. The IFSP or IEP team should consider the following when they choose an EBP:

*   The characteristics of the child and her or his family (e.g., the child’s strengths and challenges, what strategies have or have not worked in the past)
*   The student’s goal (i.e., what the student is expected to achieve and in what learning domain)
*   The expertise and experience of the teacher in successfully implementing specific EBPs
*   The availability of resources (e.g., equipment, personnel) necessary to implement a given EBP

When they select a practice to implement with a child or student, educators and practitioners should understand that:

*   When selecting a target behavior and EBP, it is important to collaborate with parents. A behavior that is problematic at school is also often problematic at home. When parents and teachers implement the same EBP, the probability that the strategy will be effective across multiple settings increases.
*   Just because a practice is deemed evidence-based does not guarantee that it will be effective for every student.
*   Information about treating and even curing autism is abundantly available on the Internet, but many of these practices are unproven, and are sometimes even harmful. For this reason, educators and practitioners should rely on trustworthy sources to identify evidence-based practices.

Once an EBP has been selected and implemented with a child, the educator or practitioner needs to collect data on the behavior to evaluate how the EBP is working for the individual student. It is also important to determine whether the EBP was implemented with _fidelity_ (i.e., implemented as the developer intended), especially if the EBP was not effective for the student. Kara Hume and Ilene Schwartz discuss selecting an EBP, implementing a practice with fidelity, and evaluating whether an EBP is effective for a student.

The National Professional Development Center (NPDC) on Autism Spectrum Disorder has identified 27 evidence-based practices for improving outcomes for students with ASD.

EBP Definition

**Antecedent-based intervention** - Arrangement of events or circumstances that precede the occurrence of an interfering behavior and designed to lead to the reduction of the behavior.

**Cognitive behavioral intervention** - Instruction on management or control of cognitive processes that lead to changes in overt behavior.

**Differential reinforcement of alternative, incompatible, or other behavior** - Provision of positive/desirable consequences for behaviors or their absence that reduce the occurrence of an undesirable behavior. Reinforcement provided: a) when the learner is engaging in a specific desired behavior other than the inappropriate behavior (DRA), b) when the learner is engaging in a behavior that is physically impossible to do while exhibiting the inappropriate behavior (DRI), or c) when the learner is not engaging in the interfering behavior (DRO).

**Discrete trial teaching** - Instructional process usually involving one teacher/service provider and one student/client and designed to teach appropriate behavior or skills. Instruction usually involves massed trials. Each trial consists of the teacher’s instruction/presentation, the child’s response, a carefully planned consequence, and a pause prior to presenting the next instruction.

**Exercise** - Increase in physical exertion as a means of reducing problem behaviors or increasing appropriate behavior.

**Extinction** - Withdrawal or removal of reinforcers of interfering behavior in order to reduce the occurrence of that behavior. Although sometimes used as a single intervention practice, extinction often occurs in combination with functional behavior assessment, functional communication training, and differential reinforcement.

**Functional behavior assessment (FBA)** - Systematic collection of information about an interfering behavior designed to identify functional contingencies that support the behavior. FBA consists of describing the interfering or problem behavior, identifying antecedent or consequent events that control the behavior, developing a hypothesis of the function of the behavior, and/or testing the hypothesis.

**Functional communication training** - Replacement of interfering behavior that has a communication function with more appropriate communication that accomplishes the same function. Functional communication training usually includes FBA, differential reinforcement of alternative behavior, and/ or extinction.

**Modeling** - Demonstration of a desired target behavior that results in imitation of the behavior by the learner and that leads to the acquisition of the imitated behavior. This EBP is often combined with other strategies such as prompting and reinforcement.

**Naturalistic intervention** - Intervention strategies that occur within the typical setting/activities/routines in which the learner participates. Teachers/service providers establish the learner’s interest in a learning event through arrangement of the setting/activity/routine, provide necessary support for the learner to engage in the targeted behavior, elaborate on the behavior when it occurs, and/or arrange natural consequences for the targeted behavior or skills.

**Parent-implemented intervention** - Parents provide individualized intervention to their child to improve/increase a wide variety of skills and/or to reduce interfering behaviors. Parents learn to deliver interventions in their home and/or community through a structured parent training program.

**Peer-mediated instruction and intervention** - Typically developing peers interact with and/or help children and youth with ASD to acquire new behavior, communication, and social skills by increasing social and learning opportunities within natural environments. Teachers/service providers systematically teach peers strategies for engaging children and youth with ASD in positive and extended social interactions in both teacher-directed and learner-initiated activities.

**Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS)** - Learners are initially taught to give a picture of a desired item to a communicative partner in exchange for the desired item. PECS consists of six phases which are: (1) “how” to communicate, (2) distance and persistence, (3) picture discrimination, (4) sentence structure, (5) responsive requesting, and (6) commenting.

**Pivotal response training** - Pivotal learning variables (i.e., motivation, responding to multiple cues, self-management, and self-initiations) guide intervention practices that are implemented in settings that build on learner interests and initiative.

**Prompting** - Verbal, gestural, or physical assistance given to learners to assist them in acquiring or engaging in a targeted behavior or skill. Prompts are generally given by an adult or peer before or as a learner attempts to use a skill.

**Reinforcement** - An event, activity, or other circumstance occurring after a learner engages in a desired behavior that leads to the increased occurrence of the behavior in the future.

**Response interruption/redirection** - Introduction of a prompt, comment, or other distracters when an interfering behavior is occurring that is designed to divert the learner’s attention away from the interfering behavior and results in its reduction.

**Scripting** - A verbal and/or written description about a specific skill or situation that serves as a model for the learner. Scripts are usually practiced repeatedly before the skill is used in the actual situation.

**Self-management** - Instruction focusing on learners discriminating between appropriate and inappropriate behaviors, accurately monitoring and recording their own behaviors, and rewarding themselves for behaving appropriately.

**Social narratives** - Narratives that describe social situations in some detail by highlighting relevant cues and offering examples of appropriate responding. Social narratives are individualized according to learner needs and typically are quite short, perhaps including pictures or other visual aids.

**Social skills training** - Group or individual instruction designed to teach learners with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) ways to appropriately interact with peers, adults, and other individuals. Most social skill meetings include instruction on basic concepts, role-playing or practice, and feedback to help learners with ASD acquire and practice communication, play, or social skills to promote positive interactions with peers.

**Structured play group** - Small group activities characterized by their occurrences in a defined area and with a defined activity, the specific selection of typically developing peers to be in the group, a clear delineation of theme and roles by adult leading, prompting, or scaffolding as needed to support students’ performance related to the goals of the activity.

**Task analysis** - A process in which an activity or behavior is divided into small, manageable steps in order to assess and teach the skill. Other practices, such as reinforcement, video modeling, or time delay, are often used to facilitate acquisition of the smaller steps.

**Technology-aided instruction and intervention (TAII)** - Instruction or interventions in which technology (e.g., tablet, computer, computer program, online activity) is used to increase or maintain functional skills and behaviors.

**Time delay** - In a setting or activity in which a learner should engage in a behavior or skill, a brief delay occurs between the opportunity to use the skill and any additional instructions or prompts. The purpose of the time delay is to allow the learner to respond without having to receive a prompt and thus focuses on fading the use of prompts during instructional activities.

**Video modeling** - A visual model of the targeted behavior or skill (typically in the behavior, communication, play, or social domains), provided via video recording and display equipment to assist learning in or engaging in a desired behavior or skill.

**Visual support** - Any visual display that supports the learner engaging in a desired behavior or skills independent of prompts. The _target behavior_ is the behavior the teacher wants to change. This should be a discrete behavior that is directly observable, measurable, and clearly defined. The definition of the behavior should:
* Describe the behavior in an observable manner
* Describe the behavior in measurable terms (i.e., instances of the behavior can be counted or timed)
* Identify the setting in which the behavior occurs

To learn more about collecting observational data on a child or student’s behavior, visit the following IRIS Case Study:
* [Measuring Behavior](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/wp-content/uploads/pdf_case_studies/ics_measbeh.pdf#content)

The goal should include information about:
* When or where the behavior will be performed
* What behavior should be displayed
* Specific, measurable criterion for mastery

Note the difference in the goals below.
1. Poorly written goal: _Michelle will respect other’s personal space_.
2. Observable goal: _When talking to friends or school personnel, Michelle will stand a minimum of 1½ feet from them at least 90% of the time_.

The next step in this process is to determine which EBPs can address the target behavior. With those in mind, educators can select an EBP that is likely to be effective for a student. The IFSP or IEP team should consider the following when they choose an EBP:
* The characteristics of the child and her or his family (e.g., the child’s strengths and challenges, what strategies have or have not worked in the past)
* The student’s goal (i.e., what the student is expected to achieve and in what learning domain)
* The expertise and experience of the teacher in successfully implementing specific EBPs
* The availability of resources (e.g., equipment, personnel) necessary to implement a given EBP

When they select a practice to implement with a child or student, educators and practitioners should understand that:

* Information about treating and even curing autism is abundantly available on the Internet, but many of these practices are unproven, and are sometimes even harmful. For this reason, educators and practitioners should rely on trustworthy sources to identify evidence-based practices.

Once an EBP has been selected and implemented with a child, the educator or practitioner needs to collect data on the behavior to evaluate how the EBP is working for the individual student. It is also important to determine whether the EBP was implemented with _fidelity_ (i.e., implemented as the developer intended), especially if the EBP was not effective for the student.",

**Reinforcement**An event, activity, or other circumstance occurring after a learner engages in a desired behavior that leads to the increased occurrence of the behavior in the future.
**Response interruption/ redirection**Introduction of a prompt, comment, or other distracters when an interfering behavior is occurring that is designed to divert the learner’s attention away from the interfering behavior and results in its reduction.

## What do educators need to know about EBPs for children with autism?

To improve the outcomes of children with ASD, educators should implement [evidence-based practices (EBPs)](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/cresource/q1/javascript_required.html), strategies that have been shown to be effective in teaching appropriate behaviors and skills and decreasing inappropriate behaviors for a given population. There are evidence-based practices to improve academic and behavior outcomes for all students. However, this module will focus on strategies that have been shown to be effective in teaching appropriate behaviors and skills and decreasing inappropriate behaviors for students with ASD. The National Professional Development Center (NPDC) on Autism Spectrum Disorder has identified 27 evidence-based practices for improving outcomes for students with ASD.

EBP Definition
**Antecedent-based intervention**Arrangement of events or circumstances that precede the occurrence of an interfering behavior and designed to lead to the reduction of the behavior.
**Cognitive behavioral intervention**Instruction on management or control of cognitive processes that lead to changes in overt behavior.
**Differential reinforcement of alternative, incompatible, or other behavior**Provision of positive/desirable consequences for behaviors or their absence that reduce the occurrence of an undesirable behavior. Reinforcement provided: a) when the learner is engaging in a specific desired behavior other than the inappropriate behavior (DRA), b) when the learner is engaging in a behavior that is physically impossible to do while exhibiting the inappropriate behavior (DRI), or c) when the learner is not engaging in the interfering behavior (DRO).
**Discrete trial teaching**Instructional process usually involving one teacher/service provider and one student/client and designed to teach appropriate behavior or skills. Instruction usually involves massed trials. Each trial consists of the teacher’s instruction/presentation, the child’s response, a carefully planned consequence, and a pause prior to presenting the next instruction.
**Exercise**Increase in physical exertion as a means of reducing problem behaviors or increasing appropriate behavior.
**Extinction**Withdrawal or removal of reinforcers of interfering behavior in order to reduce the occurrence of that behavior. Although sometimes used as a single intervention practice, extinction often occurs in combination with functional behavior assessment, functional communication training, and differential reinforcement.
**Functional behavior assessment (FBA)**Systematic collection of information about an interfering behavior designed to identify functional contingencies that support the behavior. FBA consists of describing the interfering or problem behavior, identifying antecedent or consequent events that control the behavior, developing a hypothesis of the function of the behavior, and/or testing the hypothesis.
**Functional communication training**Replacement of interfering behavior that has a communication function with more appropriate communication that accomplishes the same function. Functional communication training usually includes FBA, differential reinforcement of alternative behavior, and/ or extinction.
**Modeling**Demonstration of a desired target behavior that results in imitation of the behavior by the learner and that leads to the acquisition of the imitated behavior. This EBP is often combined with other strategies such as prompting and reinforcement.
**Naturalistic intervention**Intervention strategies that occur within the typical setting/activities/routines in which the learner participates. Teachers/service providers establish the learner’s interest in a learning event through arrangement of the setting/activity/routine, provide necessary support for the learner to engage in the targeted behavior, elaborate on the behavior when it occurs, and/or arrange natural consequences for the targeted behavior or skills.
**Parent-implemented intervention**Parents provide individualized intervention to their child to improve/increase a wide variety of skills and/or to reduce interfering behaviors. Parents learn to deliver interventions in their home and/or community through a structured parent training program.
**Peer-mediated instruction and intervention**Typically developing peers interact with and/or help children and youth with ASD to acquire new behavior, communication, and social skills by increasing social and learning opportunities within natural environments. Teachers/service providers systematically teach peers strategies for engaging children and youth with ASD in positive and extended social interactions in both teacher-directed and learner-initiated activities.
**Picture Exchange Communication System (PECS)**Learners are initially taught to give a picture of a desired item to a communicative partner in exchange for the desired item. PECS consists of six phases which are: (1) “how” to communicate, (2) distance and persistence, (3) picture discrimination, (4) sentence structure, (5) responsive requesting, and (6) commenting.
**Pivotal response training**Pivotal learning variables (i .e., motivation, responding to multiple cues, self-management, and self-initiations) guide intervention practices that are implemented in settings that build on learner interests and initiative.
**Prompting**Verbal, gestural, or physical assistance given to learners to assist them in acquiring or engaging in a targeted behavior or skill. Prompts are generally given by an adult or peer before or as a learner attempts to use a skill.
**Reinforcement**An event, activity, or other circumstance occurring after a learner engages in a desired behavior that leads to the increased occurrence of the behavior in the future.
**Response interruption/ redirection**Introduction of a prompt, comment, or other distracters when an interfering behavior is occurring that is designed to divert the learner’s attention away from the interfering behavior and results in its reduction.
**Scripting**A verbal and/or written description about a specific skill or situation that serves as a model for the learner. Scripts are usually practiced repeatedly before the skill is used in the actual situation
**Self-management**Instruction focusing on learners discriminating between appropriate and inappropriate behaviors, accurately monitoring and recording their own behaviors, and rewarding themselves for behaving appropriately.
**Social narratives**Narratives that describe social situations in some detail by highlighting relevant cues and offering examples of appropriate responding. Social narratives are individualized according to learner needs and typically are quite short, perhaps including pictures or other visual aids.
**Social skills training**Group or individual instruction designed to teach learners with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) ways to appropriately interact with peers, adults, and other individuals. Most social skill meetings include instruction on basic concepts, role-playing or practice, and feedback to help learners with ASD acquire and practice communication, play, or social skills to promote positive interactions with peers.
**Structured play group**Small group activities characterized by their occurrences in a defined area and with a defined activity, the specific selection of typically developing peers to be in the group, a clear delineation of theme and roles by adult leading, prompting, or scaffolding as needed to support students’ performance related to the goals of the activity.
**Task analysis**A process in which an activity or behavior is divided into small, manageable steps in order to assess and teach the skill. Other practices, such as reinforcement, video modeling, or time delay, are often used to facilitate acquisition of the smaller steps.
**Technology-aided instruction and intervention (TAII)**Instruction or interventions in which technology (e.g., tablet, computer, computer program, online activity) is used to increase or maintain functional skills and behaviors.
**Time delay**In a setting or activity in which a learner should engage in a behavior or skill, a brief delay occurs between the opportunity to use the skill and any additional instructions or prompts. The purpose of the time delay is to allow the learner to respond without having to receive a prompt and thus focuses on fading the use of prompts during instructional activities .
**Video modeling**A visual model of the targeted behavior or skill (typically in the behavior, communication, play, or social domains), provided via video recording and display equipment to assist learning in or engaging in a desired behavior or skill .
**Visual support**Any visual display that supports the learner engaging in a desired behavior or skills independent of prompts. Examples of visual supports include pictures, written words, objects within the environment, arrangement of the environment or visual boundaries, schedules, maps, labels, organization systems, and timelines.

[Click here to download and save a PDF version of the list](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/wp-content/uploads/modules/asd2/pdf/asd2_27ebp_definitions.pdf#content).

With so many EBPs from which to choose, how can educators or practitioners determine which of them to use with a specific child? The four steps outlined below can help educators and practitioners make a more informed decision when they select an EBP.

The _target behavior_ is the behavior the teacher wants to change. This should be a discrete behavior that is directly observable, measurable, and clearly defined. The definition of the behavior should:

*   Describe the behavior in an observable manner
*   Describe the behavior in measurable terms (i.e., instances of the behavior can be counted or timed)
*   Identify the setting in which the behavior occurs

Note the difference in the definitions below.

1.   Ambiguous and subjective definition: _Michelle violates other’s personal space_.
2.   Clear and observable definition: _When talking to someone, Michelle stands within a foot of that person_.

Defining behavior in this manner allows multiple professionals to observe and collect objective data on the behavior. If multiple professionals gather data using the second definition of Michelle’s behavior, they are more likely to collect data on the same behavior rather than on their subjective opinion of personal space violation.

To learn more about how to clearly define a student’s behavior so that when it occurs it can be reliably identified, measured, or counted, visit the following IRIS Case Study:

*   [Defining Behavior](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/wp-content/uploads/pdf_case_studies/ics_defbeh.pdf#content)

_Baseline data_ refers to the level (i.e., frequency, duration) at which a behavior occurs before a strategy or intervention is implemented. These data should be gathered for at least four days or until a pattern of behavior is evident. By comparing these data to data collected after the strategy has been implemented, educators can determine whether it is effective for the student.

To learn more about collecting observational data on a child or student’s behavior, visit the following IRIS Case Study:

*   [Measuring Behavior](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/wp-content/uploads/pdf_case_studies/ics_measbeh.pdf#content)

Once the target behavior has been identified and baseline data collected, the goal needs to be indicated in a child’s [individualized education program (IEP)](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/cresource/q1/javascript_required.html) or [individualized family service plan (IFSP)](https://iris.peabody.vanderbilt.edu/module/asd2/cresource/q1/javascript_required.html). The goal should include information about:

*   When or where the behavior will be performed
*   What behavior should be displayed
*   Specific, measurable criterion for mastery

Note the difference in the goals below.

1.   Poorly written goal: _Michelle will respect other’s personal space_.
2.   Observable goal: _When talking to friends or school personnel, Michelle will stand a minimum of 1½ feet from them at least 90% of the time_.

The next step in this process is to determine which EBPs can address the target behavior. With those in mind, educators can select an EBP that is likely to be effective for a student. The IFSP or IEP team should consider the following when they choose an EBP:

*   The characteristics of the child and her or his family (e.g., the child’s strengths and challenges, what strategies have or have not worked in the past)
*   The student’s goal (i.e., what the student is expected to achieve and in what learning domain)
*   The expertise and experience of the teacher in successfully implementing specific EBPs
*   The availability of resources (e.g., equipment, personnel) necessary to implement a given EBP

When they select a practice to implement with a child or student, educators and practitioners should understand that:

*   When selecting a target behavior and EBP, it is important to collaborate with parents. A behavior that is problematic at school is also often problematic at home. When parents and teachers implement the same EBP, the probability that the strategy will be effective across multiple settings increases.
*   Just because a practice is deemed evidence-based does not guarantee that it will be effective for every student.
*   Information about treating and even curing autism is abundantly available on the Internet, but many of these practices are unproven, and are sometimes even harmful. For this reason, educators and practitioners should rely on trustworthy sources to identify evidence-based practices.

Once an EBP has been selected and implemented with a child, the educator or practitioner needs to collect data on the behavior to evaluate how the EBP is working for the individual student. It is also important to determine whether the EBP was implemented with _fidelity_ (i.e., implemented as the developer intended), especially if the EBP was not effective for the student. Kara Hume and Ilene Schwartz discuss selecting an EBP, implementing a practice with fidelity, and evaluating whether an EBP is effective for a student.

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Autism in the classroom: Strategies for success

Markdown Content:
School Community Tool Kit

![Image 1: Colorful classroom for young children](https://www.autismspeaks.org/sites/default/files/styles/wysiwyg_medium_width/public/helping-special-needs-students-in-the-classroom.jpg?itok=5nC3xjnb)

## Strategies for success when teaching students with autism

1.   **Be calm and positive.**Model appropriate behavior for the student with autism, as well as for other students, by greeting him and engaging him in a respectful way.
2.   **Be aware of the characteristics of autism and general strategies** - for quick reference reminders use the resources included in the[School Community Tool Kit](https://www.autismspeaks.org/tool-kit/school-community-tool-kit).
3.   **Use the “About Me” information sheet**to get to know relevant facts about each particular student’s likes, fears, needs, etc.
    *   Ask specific questions regarding safety and impulsivity. If you haven’t received one, ask the school team whether there is an “About Me” information sheet available for each student with autism in your classroom.

4.   **Promote a welcoming environment**, and provide opportunities for your student (and others!) to develop social interaction skills and extended learning
5.   **Teach understanding and acceptance**—see the Resources section of this kit for suggested reading, including books and programs to use with the students.
    *   Pair the student with peers who are positive role models
    *   Allow times for students to work in pairs and/or small groups
    *   Be aware that students with autism can become isolated within the classroom (interaction only occurring between an aide and student) and be on the lookout to prevent it by working with the students and the paraprofessional to support social exchange among peers

6.   **Students with autism may not be socially savvy**; therefore, if a student is being bullied or tortured quietly, he is likely to react or respond – but may not do so in a way that seems appropriate or is easy to recognize. Consider the student’s communication difficulties and make every attempt to fully understand the situation before reaching judgment regarding fault or behavior.
7.   **Ensure that organization, communication and sensory issues are addressed** (see the General Strategies and Classroom Checklist in the [School Community Tool Kit](https://www.autismspeaks.org/tool-kit/school-community-tool-kit))
8.   **Establish clear routines and habits** to support regular activities and transitions. Alert the student to changes in routine, staffing, etc., in advance, whenever possible.
9.   **Consider seating** - situate the student for optimal attention to instruction or sensory needs
10.   **Pay particular attention to the general strategies outlined for supporting communication** and organization (simple directions, wait-time for processing verbal requests or directions, visual schedules, prompts and cues, etc.)
11.   **Be tuned into sensory issues**that may effect the student in your particular class (for example, echoing locker rooms and loud, fast activity can make P.E. over-stimulating and overwhelming)
12.   **Provide written rules or pictures of expectations of behavior in the classroom**, including ‘unwritten’ conventions if necessary. Work with the student’s team to incorporate social narratives to help a student understand a rule or expectation. Learners with autism often increase compliance if they understand why a rule exists (for example, It is important to remain quiet - no noise or talking - while the teacher is speaking. If it is noisy, the students will not be able to hear her.).
13.   **Use descriptive praise to build desired behaviors** (for example, ‘I like the way you put your trash in the trash can!’)
14.   **Give positive directions**; minimize the use of ‘don’t’ and ‘stop.’ ‘Please sit in your seat’ can be more effective than ‘Don’t stand up.’ This lets the student know exactly what you would like him to do.

**Learn strategies for success for teachers by subject, as well as all members of the school community, in the**[**Autism Speaks School Community Tool Kit**](https://www.autismspeaks.org/tool-kit/school-community-tool-kit)**.**

## **Webpage Content** 
Title: Structured Teaching Strategies for Students on the Autism Spectrum

URL Source: https://readingrockets.org/topics/autism-spectrum-disorder/articles/structured-teaching-strategies-students-autism-spectrum

Markdown Content:
This series of four articles can be used as a set or separately depending on the needs of the staff/students. Each article will review the rationale for the use of structured teaching, as well provide as a brief description of the TEACCH model.

## Structured Teaching: an overview

Structured Teaching is a set of teaching techniques developed by Division TEACCH (**T**raining and **E**ducation of **A**utistic and related **C**ommunication-handicapped **C**hildren), a state-wide program serving individuals with autism spectrum disorders (ASD) in North Carolina.

Division TEACCH is a comprehensive treatment model that serves individuals with autism across the lifespan. Along with the structured teaching strategies, the model emphasizes an extensive understanding of autism, partnering with families, individualized assessment when developing and implementing strategies, and the development of skills across curriculum areas (with attention to the development of communication and social skills).

Structured teaching strategies can be implemented across settings and across curriculum area, as they serve as a vehicle to teach skills, and/or as a framework for a classroom setting.

These teaching strategies are based on an understanding of how autism impacts the thinking, learning, and behavior of an individual with ASD. Differences in auditory processing, imitation, motivation, and organization can hinder the educational success of students with ASD, as most traditional teaching strategies rely heavily on verbal instructions, demonstration, social reinforcement, and sequencing chunks of information or directives.

Structured Teaching strategies, however, capitalize on the strengths of students with ASD. These include providing predictable and meaningful routines through the use of structure, adding visual/structural supports to classroom instruction and activities to increase engagement and independence, and clearly organizing classroom spaces and teaching materials to reduce anxiety and increase appropriate behavior.

There are five elements of Structured Teaching that build on one another, and all emphasize the importance of predictability and flexible routines in the classroom setting. Division TEACCH developed a visual to illustrate the Structured Teaching components — the Structured Teaching pyramid:

![Image 1](https://readingrockets.org/sites/default/files/migrated/images/articles/Structured%20Teaching%20Pyramid.png)

## Article 1: Physical structure in the school setting

This article describes the [physical structure](https://readingrockets.org/article/physical-structure-school-setting) component of the Structured Teaching pyramid. Physical structure is the foundation of structured teaching and is helpful in ensuring that learning is occurring in the classroom.

## Article 2: Visual schedules in the school setting

This article describes the [visual schedule](https://readingrockets.org/article/visual-schedules-school-setting) component of the Structured Teaching pyramid. A visual schedule communicates the sequence of upcoming activities or events through the use of objects, photographs, icons, words, or a combination of tangible supports.

## Article 3: Work systems in the school setting

This article describes the [work systems](https://readingrockets.org/article/work-systems-school-setting) component of the Structured Teaching pyramid. A work system is an organizational system that gives a student with ASD information about what is expected when he/she arrives at a classroom location.

## Article 4: Visual structure in the school setting

This article describes the [visual structure](https://readingrockets.org/article/visual-structure-school-setting) component of the Structured Teaching pyramid. Visual structure adds a physical or visual component to tasks to assist students in understanding HOW an activity should be completed.
